title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
One workflow for every dataset
Learn one workflow, then repeat it with a different dataset. Start with the required workspace setup and follow the synthetic practice in order. Use the same seven steps for DietSwap, Mouse59, and your own study.

text:

title: AI-Assisted Microbiome Analysis
text:
The datasets







Dataset
What you will learn




Synthetic practice
Read and check results from 24 samples and 15 fictional features


DietSwap
Describe a selected cohort comparison using 38 participant samples


Mouse59
Explore 59 samples and 2,027 OTUs, including low-count samples


Your own study
Prepare three tidy TSV files and apply the same workflow









Note



Setup is required before running the workflow. Each dataset follows the same page structure. Its question, input/output folders, and dataset-specific details change; the analysis steps stay the same.


The guide starts from prepared feature tables and produces descriptive results. Raw sequencing processing and statistical hypothesis testing require additional workflows.
Next: Set up your workspace

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Before you begin
Complete this setup before beginning the guide. You will download the project files, open your workspace, and restore the R packages needed for all three examples.
Work through the sections in order. You only need to complete this setup once.
Have R, Quarto, and an editor such as VS Code or RStudio installed on your computer.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Get the project files
Download the project ZIP

Extract the downloaded ZIP.
Open the extracted ai-assisted-microbiome-analysis-main folder in VS Code or RStudio.
Open a terminal in that folder.







Note



This is your project folder, also called the repository root. It contains _quarto.yml, renv.lock, data/, scripts/. Run the guide’s terminal commands from this folder.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Restore the R environment
The project includes renv.lock, which records the R packages used for the supplied analyses.






Where does code run?



Run terminal commands such as R, Rscript, and quarto in your terminal. After starting R, run R expressions at the R prompt (>). Opening a guide page does not run its code.


In the terminal, start R:
R
At the R prompt (>), run:
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("renv")
}

renv::restore()
renv::status()
If asked to proceed, enter Y and wait for the > prompt before entering another command. Restore the supplied lockfile rather than initializing a new environment.
Check that the analysis packages load, then return to the terminal:
library(tidyverse)
library(vegan)

q(save = "no")






Note



If setup fails: copy the error message. Ask AI to explain it using your R version, operating system, and the command you ran. Check the proposed fix before applying it. Keep the supplied lockfile intact while investigating.

title: Set up your workspace
text:
Ready to begin?
Your terminal should be open in the project root, renv::status() should report no synchronization issues, and both packages should load successfully.

title: 2. Preview the results: Synthetic practice
text:
Composition



Composition in Synthetic practice. Each bar shows relative feature proportions for one sample; remaining features are pooled as Other.


The supplied composition figure shows a generally larger pooled Other fraction in Group B. Other pools seven fictional features, so its size does not identify which individual features contribute to the pattern. Check their proportions in the unpooled table.
Open the composition image at full size to read its labels.
crumbs: 4  2. Preview the results: Synthetic practice

title: 2. Preview the results: Synthetic practice
text:
Shannon diversity



Shannon diversity in Synthetic practice. Each point is one sample; Shannon uses the full feature table.


The supplied table has median Shannon values of about 2.428 in Group A and 2.560 in Group B. All samples have 15 observed features, so this difference reflects evenness in their feature proportions.
crumbs: 4  2. Preview the results: Synthetic practice

title: 2. Preview the results: Synthetic practice
text:
Count totals and diversity



Count totals and diversity in Synthetic practice. Each point relates one sample’s feature-table count total to its Shannon diversity.


Compare count ranges within and between groups. Samples with similar totals can have different feature proportions and Shannon values.






Note



These are descriptive plots. Composition bars sum to 100%; they do not show count totals. Visual differences alone do not establish statistical significance or causation.

crumbs: 9  7. Write the report: Synthetic practice

title: 7. Write the report: Synthetic practice
text:
Copy this outline
---
title: "Synthetic practice: microbiome analysis"
format: html
execute:
  eval: false
---

## Question and dataset

Replace this paragraph with your question, group labels, sample and feature counts, and what each sample represents. Record any unavailable study information.

## Inputs and decisions

Inputs: `data/example/`. Outputs: `results/example/`.

Describe the selected samples, feature labels, and any exclusions or changes. State that the workflow produces descriptive summaries.

## Composition

![Feature composition by sample.](results/example/figures/composition.png)

Describe one pattern and support it with feature proportions from the saved table. Explain what is pooled as Other.

## Shannon diversity

![Shannon diversity by group.](results/example/figures/shannon-diversity.png)

Report group medians and describe spread and overlap. Check observed feature counts before explaining the pattern.

## Count totals and diversity

![Count totals and Shannon diversity.](results/example/figures/depth-diversity.png)

Describe count ranges and unusual samples. Check the corresponding sample rows in the diversity table.

## Checks

Name the table values you checked. If you performed the optional sample verification, report the sample ID, total, observed features, Shannon, and agreement.

## Conclusion and limitations

Answer the question within the scope of these samples. State one limitation and a next question. Visual differences alone do not establish significance or causation.

## Reproducibility and AI assistance

Record the analysis command, input/output folders, decisions, and location of `session-info.txt`. State how AI was used and checked, or state that it was not used.

What the scripts do







Script in scripts/R/
Purpose

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference and glossary
text:
Terms used in the figures







Term
Meaning in this workflow




Feature
A row in the count table, such as an OTU or another supplied microbial feature


OTU
Operational taxonomic unit; a sequence-based feature whose identifier alone does not name a species


Count total
Sum of all feature counts in one sample; not a measure of total microbial biomass


Relative proportion
Feature count divided by that sample’s count total


Observed features
Number of features with a positive count in one sample


Richness
Number of distinct features; observed richness counts those detected in the supplied sample


Evenness
How evenly a sample’s counts are distributed among its features


Shannon diversity
A summary reflecting richness and evenness, using natural logarithms


Other
All features outside the top eight, pooled only for the composition display

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference and glossary
text:
How Shannon is calculated
For a sample with feature counts \(x_i\), calculate each proportion as \(p_i=x_i/\sum_j x_j\). Then:
\[
H=-\sum_{i:p_i>0} p_i\ln(p_i).
\]
Zero proportions contribute zero and are omitted from the logarithm calculation. Shannon uses all features in the supplied analysis table. The top-eight selection and pooled Other category are used only for composition plotting.
If every feature count in a sample is multiplied by the same positive factor, its proportions and Shannon value remain unchanged. In observed sequencing data, however, low counts can limit detection of features; investigate unusually low totals before interpreting diversity.

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference and glossary
text:

Output within the selected results folder
Use




tables/alpha-diversity.tsv
Check sample totals, observed features, and Shannon


tables/relative-abundance.tsv
Check individual feature proportions


tables/composition-display.tsv
Inspect the features selected for display and pooled Other


tables/group-summary.tsv
Check group summaries


figures/
View composition, Shannon diversity, and count-total plots


session-info.txt
Record R and package versions



Composition bars sum to 100%. A feature’s proportion can change when other features change, so proportions alone do not measure absolute abundance. Compare variation within groups as well as differences between them.

title: Appendix A — Workflow reference and glossary
text:
Reporting and interpretation
Each dataset’s final page provides a copyable report outline, matching figure paths, a report filename, and the render command. Save the report QMD in the project root so its relative image paths resolve correctly.
Rendering uses existing analysis outputs. If inputs change, rerun the dataset’s analysis before rendering the report. After an error, resolve the problem before interpreting files that may remain from an earlier run.
The supplied workflow produces descriptive summaries. Visual differences alone do not establish statistical significance or causation. Paired observations, repeated visits, shared cages, confounding, and statistical inference need additional decisions and methods appropriate to the study.
If AI helps draft an explanation, check its numbers, group labels, and claims against the supplied outputs. Record which suggestions you accepted or revised and why.
